tables.h2: 6 · Subnet address, broadcast address and VLAN ID: three different things
rows: Defines an IP address range and routing boundary using CIDR; not an application protocol or peer identity
192.168.10.0/24 covers addresses in that IPv4 subnet
Targets hosts in an IPv4 subnet if supported/permitted; often blocked across routers
802.1Q tag identifying a Layer-2 broadcast domain on participating links; local to network design
VLAN 20 for lab machines, VLAN 30 for staff devices
Layer-2 interface address used in Ethernet forwarding
Switch learns source MAC per VLAN and forwards frames
IP address + transport protocol + port, with connection context

tables.h2: 8 · Protocols: HTTP, gRPC, MQTT, AMQP and QUIC
rows: Datagram transport; no built-in reliability guarantee
Secure multiplexed transport over UDP with built-in TLS 1.3
HTTP application semantics; REST is an architectural style, not a separate transport protocol
RPC framework commonly using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers; other transports exist
Lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol, usually broker-based
Messaging protocol family; details depend on version and broker
Bidirectional application messaging over a persistent connection

tables.h2: 11 · Correction ledger: original assertion → explanation → evidence
rows: “Request-response uses subnet ID and VLAN ID”
HTTP API requests use routable network endpoints; an HTTPS client on cellular can reach a cloud API without a shared VLAN.
“Message-driven needs broadcast ID and broker subnet”
MQTT or AMQP broker messaging normally uses IP unicast; cloud publishers and subscribers may live on different subnets.
Peers can use signaling/tracker/relay servers; WebRTC often uses STUN/TURN.
They are specific NAT traversal/relay tools; LAN P2P and other overlay designs may not use them.
Broadcast is an IPv4 network delivery mechanism, not an application endpoint identity.
Fiber/copper are media; switches are active devices.
These are virtual networking systems or abstractions that ultimately depend on physical media.
